slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1870 census (Ninth Census) aged to November 1872, men 21+ outside the former Confederate states; the Fifteenth Amendment now let Black men vote everywhere; calibrated to certified returns.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: No women could vote for president in 1872 (some who tried, in Rochester and elsewhere, were arrested); women 21+ shown for population only.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1870 census aged to 1872, white adults in the former Confederate states, all now readmitted and voting by popular vote; most former Confederates had their disabilities lifted by the May 1872 amnesty; calibrated to certified returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1870 census aged to 1872, Black adults in the former Confederate states; Black men voted under the Fifteenth Amendment and the federal Enforcement Acts, which had broken up much of the Klan by 1872.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: 1870 census aged to 1872, foreign-born white men not yet naturalized; many Midwestern, Western and Southern states let declarant aliens vote, elsewhere only naturalized men could.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1872 comes out as it did: Grant wins, 286–66. The closest state was Virginia, which went to Grant by 0.4 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1870 and 1880 census counts interpolated to 1872 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1872 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

everyone.summary: 13.1 million more adults vote. Greeley wins, 160–192. The closest call is Nevada, which holds for Grant by 1.3 points. Greeley wins in 73 of 100 draws.
assumptions: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1872.
howIGotThis: What changed: Every adult can vote, and turns out.
New voters borrow the behaviour of naturalized citizens of the same state and sex; Black voters outside the South.
The numbers: the 1870 and 1880 census counts interpolated to 1872 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1872 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: I wish I could have my say tomorrow, but the law doesn't allow women to vote. That's how it is.
south-white.controlQuote: I wish I could have my say tomorrow, but the law doesn't allow women to vote. That's how it is.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I cannot vote—the law doesn't allow it. My husband will cast our household's ballot tomorrow.
women.controlQuote: I cannot vote—the law doesn't allow it. My husband will cast our household's ballot tomorrow.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: These thieving officials in Washington make my blood boil, but I cannot trust the other side to protect the colored man's rights or keep the peace in the South.
